[Editors’ note: this article was originally rejected after discussions between the reviewers, but the authors were invited to resubmit after an appeal against the decision.]

Thank you for choosing to send your work entitled "Frequency-selective control of forebrain networks by central thalamus" for consideration at eLife. Your full submission has been evaluated by Timothy Behrens (Senior Editor), Andrew King (Reviewing Editor) and three peer reviewers, and the decision was reached after discussions between the reviewers. Based on our discussions and the individual reviews below, we regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife.

Although we were impressed with the interdisciplinary approach used in this study, particularly the combination of optical stimulation and fMRI, as well as its potential therapeutic implications, a number of significant concerns were raised by the reviewers. While some of these can be dealt with by changes to the text, other methodological concerns will likely require further experiments. In particular, the effects of varying the frequency of optical stimulation appear to be confounded by changes in pulse duration and number. Two of the reviewers also felt that the section on the zona incerta was particularly weak.

Reviewer #1:

Liu and colleagues have used a combination of fMRI, optogenetics, electrophysiology and video EEG monitoring in a rodent model to map thalamocortical and forebrain neural circuits. This work has several important contributions. The authors show that mode of stimulation can change response patterns of neurons dramatically in these central circuits. In one case, high-frequency stimulation of excitatory relay neurons in the central thalamus caused a widespread positive BOLD signal in multiple forebrain regions.

In contrast, low frequency (10 Hz) stimulation led to less neural circuit modulation, negative BOLD signal in the somatosensory cortex and loss of consciousness. This low frequency stimulation was also associated with spindle like activity in the zona incerta. The authors postulate that the zona incerta may be playing a roll in the inhibition and spindling through a feedback circuit with the central thalamus.

The authors' work suggests that negative BOLD signals could be associated with large scale inhibition in brain networks.

The work draws a compelling distinction between stimulating at a given frequency and observing population spiking activity at a given frequency after stimulation. The optogenetics disambiguate these two factors by allowing the stimulation of a specific neuronal population.

Finally, the work has enormous translational potential. The authors demonstrate substantial forebrain network activation with stimulation of the central thalamus. This observation clearly speaks to the potential use of these findings to guide developmental work on DBS for therapeutic purposes. In particular, the authors show that changing frequency of stimulation can change the brain response from broad activation of forebrain circuits for high frequency stimulation to decreased arousal and negative BOLD signals for low frequency stimulation. One could imagine using the first stimulation pattern or patterns similar to it help enhance arousal in patients who are minimally conscious or in a vegetative states, whereas the second pattern might prove useful for treating seizures. At any rate, the results offer a principled way to investigate the basic science of DBS and to learn more about the brain's arousal circuits by combining two modalities.

The manuscript is well-written. It is a significant basic neuroscience and translational neuroscience contribution. I have no major concerns.

Reviewer #2:

In this study, Liu et al carry out a multilevel exploration of the role of central thalamus activation in the control of brain states. By using optogenetic activation of the central thalamus in combination with fMRI (and other techniques), they demonstrate how the activation of somas in the central thalamus is enough to induce large changes in cortical BOLD signal, later correlated with single unit firing. The authors demonstrate that while high (40-100 Hz) frequency stimulation of the central thalamus activates different cortical (and subcortical) areas causing arousal, low (10 Hz) frequencies reduce cortical activity. The responses of zona incerta to the same stimulation patterns are compatible with a potential role of this area in the switch between both effects, at least those concerning some areas of the cortex. Even when a definitive causal and mechanistic relationship is not established, the study is relevant for both basic neuroscience – it brings together the single neuron level to the whole brain activation and it gives a feasible systems level interpretation of the phenomena – and also for the applied, clinical implications.

Main concerns:

1) The inclusion of the zona incerta as a potential intermediary of the cortical inhibition at 10 Hz provides a potential mechanism and it is valuable. However the study of this is not well justified in the text. It is not even mentioned in the Introduction and it is not well justified in the Abstract. Why the zona incerta? What inputs does it receive? Is central thalamus projecting to zona incerta? For example in the Introduction all these explanations are given for the pallidum, but then the zona incerta is the one included in the study. In the anatomical study reported in the manuscript, the ZI is never mentioned as a place of distribution of the EYFP axons.

2) In the subsection “Low-frequency central thalamus stimulation drives incertal oscillations” it is said that ZI sends direct gabaergic projections to sensory cortex (somatosensory; Nicolelis, Chaplin and Lin, 1995), and the study is carried out by recording from S1 and Z1. However, this does not explain how the brain state switch would be in prefrontal cortex or other cortical areas. It is possible that the authors have considered this and therefore it should be explicitly discussed in the text.

3) In the study of ZI the 10 Hz thalamic stimulation evokes spike and wave discharges in the EEG but this is not reported in the other recordings in the cortex during 10 Hz stim. 10 Hz CT stimulation is reported silencing the cortex, however spike and wave is a rather visible activity that does not silence the neurons. Shouldn't the spike and wave be seen in the single unit recordings?

4) Subsection “Stimulation of central thalamus relay neurons drives widespread forebrain activation in vivo”, fourth paragraph: stimulating at different frequencies always has the problem of giving the same number of pulses versus giving the stimulation for the same period of time. I understand that here the second option was taken. This means that the number of pulses was (in 6 minutes) 1200 when at 10 Hz, 4800 when at 40 Hz and 12000 at 100 Hz. In order to rule out the effect of the differential number of pulses, and since there are six blocks of repetitions, it would strengthen the conclusions to demonstrate that the differences in cortical activation remain for equivalent number of pulses. Probably the authors already have some data showing this that could be included in a supplemental figure. It is also confusing that Figure 4B shows stimulation periods that are variable and therefore (probably) adjusted to number of pulses. Was a different protocol used in this case?

5) In general there is a lack of description of the control (pre-stimulus) activity. Is the departing point slow wave activity? Is the decrease in firing during 10 Hz stimulation independent from the pre-existing activity patterns?

Reviewer #3:

This study deals with an interesting issue, the role of central thalamic nuclei in controlling cortical activation. However, there are several problems with this paper.

First, the authors seem to have a poor understanding of the effects that thalamic stimulation delivered at different frequencies has on the cortex. This has been studied previously but there is very little reflection of that knowledge here. I can think of a series of studies in the rat that investigated the cortical effects of frequency-dependent electrical stimulation in the VL/VA thalamic region (adjacent to the targeted CL/PC region) in rats. Those studies showed that stimulation in various thalamic nuclei evoke short-latency frequency-depend excitatory cortical responses that can augment (spreading significantly when stimulating in VL/VA) or depress (when stimulating in VPM/VPL). Importantly, at 10 Hz, stimulation always drives strong long-lasting feedforward inhibition, which hyperpolarizes cortical cells immediately after each short-latency excitatory response (e.g. see Fig. 1 in Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1996b). This inhibition of cortical cells may explain the negative BOLD observed in S1 during 10 Hz stimulation (20 sec); under this stimulation regimen, cortical cells will be hyperpolarized most of the time.

Second, the idea that the suppression of neural activity observed at 10 Hz would be caused by the zona incerta seems unlikely. There are numerous other possibilities. For example, the very robust drive of feedforward inhibition in neocortex at 10 Hz is more parsimonious. In general, this part of the study is very unconvincing.

Third, there are significant methodological issues to consider. Most important is the fact that the authors chose to keep the duty cycle constant across stimulation frequencies. This means that at 10 Hz the light stimulus per cycle lasts 30 ms and at 100 Hz it lasts 3 ms. This is very problematic because the changes that are being attributed to frequency can easily be attributed to pulse duration, which has very significant effects on the responses evoked. Thus, everywhere in the paper where the authors allude to frequency, they are also changing pulse duration, which is a major confound. The only reasonable way to keep the total light duration constant when studying frequency is by increasing the train duration for the lower frequencies and keeping the pulse duration constant.

Fourth, the selectivity of the stimulation, which is based mostly on the placement of the fiber, is a major limitation because the nuclei that are targeted are very small and have complex shapes. It seems inevitable that adjacent structures will also be driven by the light. A Cre-mouse that would limit the expression to the targeted nuclei would be a much better choice in this particular case.

Fifth, regarding the idea that the thalamus serves to drive cortical activation, previous work has shown that neuromodulation of neural activity in sensory thalamus leads to activation or deactivation in the related sensory cortex (Hirata and Castro-Alamancos, 2010). This work is directly related to the study at hand but was not considered here.

[Editors’ note: what now follows is the decision letter after the authors submitted for further consideration.]

Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Frequency-selective control of forebrain networks by central thalamus" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Tim Behrens (Senior Editor) and Andrew King (Reviewing Editor).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Several of their original concerns have been satisfactorily addressed in the revised version and the reviewers have acknowledged the improvements made to the manuscript, particularly through the inclusion of the new pulse width and train duration imaging data. Nevertheless, some substantive issues remain that need to be addressed before a final decision can be made (references cited are given below).

1) One of the reviewers argues that your claim that the ZI is the source of cortical inhibition during 10 Hz stimulation is still not well supported. Whilst agreeing that thalamocortical responses evoked in the sensory cortices by stimulating the sensory thalamus at 10 Hz are depressed both in vivo (Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1996b) and in slices (Cruikshank et al., 2010), the reviewer has pointed out that thalamocortical responses evoked in neocortex by stimulating other thalamic nuclei (midline, intralaminar, and VA/VL) are different in most respects, both in vivo (Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1996b) and in slices (Cruikshank et al., 2012). Stimulation of these other thalamic nuclei in vivo at 10 Hz produces facilitating (spindle-like) responses in cortex, not depressing responses. In fact, work in slices also supports this. A direct quote from the in vitro paper (Cruikshank et al., 2012) cited by the authors in the rebuttal emphasizes this, "responses during repetitive stimulation were far more sustained for matrix than for core sensory TC pathways".

Since the 1940s it has been known that stimulating thalamic nuclei at different frequencies evokes three main types of responses in cortex (Dempsey and Morison): primary responses, augmenting responses and recruiting responses. A more recent account of this literature, including more recent studies done in the rat (Dempsey and Morison worked in cats), is presented in Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1997 (not cited by the authors, but highly relevant). Primary responses occur when specific thalamic nuclei are stimulated, such as sensory thalamus. Primary responses depress with frequency. Augmenting and recruiting responses occur when VL, VA, VM, midline or intralaminar thalamic nuclei are stimulated. These responses are similar in that they produce enhanced cortical responses at stimulation frequencies between 7-14 Hz. They differ in their cortical depth profile, indicating that they target different layers (as expected from the known projections), and in the size of the primary response they evoke. VL stimulation evokes augmenting responses with a small primary response (small compared to sensory pathways) in motor cortical areas, which is surface positive. In contrast, recruiting responses are mostly surface negative, lacking the surface positive primary response of augmenting responses. The present study did not record field potential responses in cortex, so it is difficult to know if the responses they evoke at 10 Hz in cortex are augmenting or recruiting. But a consistent finding from intracellular recordings is that strong feedforward inhibition is evoked in cortex in vivo by stimulating the thalamus at 10 Hz (Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1996c; Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1996a). In fact, the area stimulated by the authors is known to evoke recruiting responses, which should yield feedforward inhibitory responses with weaker short-latency excitation (surface positivity) than augmenting responses.

The reviewer concludes that by citing papers based on specific thalamic nuclei, such as core sensory thalamic nuclei (Cruikshank et al., 2010), is not appropriate, because it is well known that the pathways stimulated in this study have different response properties.

2) The reviewer has also criticized your argument that high frequency activity evokes increased levels of interneuron-driven cortical inhibition relative to excitation, whereas low frequency activity does not, on the grounds that the relevance of the cited paper (Galarreta and Hestrin, 1998) to the issue at hand is doubtful because this study only deals with inhibition driven by cortical stimuli, not thalamic stimuli. You need to look at feedforward inhibition driven by thalamic stimulation, preferably in vivo. The other cited slice paper (Cruikshank et al., 2012), looked at feedforward inhibition driven by thalamic inputs but only marginally (only 1 example panel in Figure 6D and no group data). It is hard to derive any strong conclusions other than to say that inhibition is there, albeit depressed compared to the 1st stimulus.

3) The reviewer also points out that white matter stimulation does not mimic thalamic stimulation, let alone central thalamus stimulation, so this should not be used as an argument for the effects of thalamic stimulation on cortical activity.

4) In response to your comment that, in contrast to Fig. 1 in Castro-Alamancos and Connors (1996b), you did not observe spikes on every stimulus presentation at 10 Hz, the reviewer points out that this is based on VL stimulation and recording in the motor cortex, which evokes an augmenting response. If in that figure (or Fig. 3 of the same paper) the surface positive field potential component and associated corresponding excitatory drive (which produces the spikes) are eliminated, what is left is a recruiting response, as defined originally by Dempsey and Morison. Similar to spindles, recruiting responses trigger spikes only on some of the waves at 10 Hz. Thus, 3.6 Hz would be consistent with this. It would be helpful if you were to present PSTHs using each stimulus of the 10 Hz train as the marker (Figure 3D).

5) Your evidence that inhibition of the zona incerta during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation reverses the cortical inhibition effect is based on AAV delivery of halorhodopsin, which will not discriminate between inhibitory and excitatory neurons. Consequently, light delivery might not only inhibit ZI cells, but other cells too, including adjacent thalamocortical cells. It is therefore possible that the effects observed are due to inhibition of thalamocortical cells. Similarly, could the mCherry fibers observed in cortex actually be thalamocortical fibers? It is also possible that your stimulation could be activating the NRt, which would drive the observed spindles and the recruiting responses in the cortex at 10 Hz, in which case there would be no need for the extrinsic inhibition purportedly provided by ZI. These possibilities should be addressed in the paper. Unless they can be ruled out, conclusions about the role of the zona incerta should be modified accordingly.

6) In discussing alternative hypotheses of the mechanism of cortical inhibition, including disynaptic thalamocortical inhibition (see Discussion, paragraph four) and disynaptic corticocortical inhibition (see Discussion, paragraph six), you should include relevant literature (e.g. rat in vivo thalamic stimulation), instead of marginally related work (slice studies that used white-matter or cortical stimulation, hippocampal studies, etc.). Care should also be taken to cite the literature accurately. For example, you argue that "central thalamus at different frequencies can lead to distinct behavioral responses" and cite Morison and Dempsey (1942), but Dempsey and Morison did not study behavior. Galarreta and Hestrin (1998) did not study thalamocortical responses (please correct this in the subsection “Central thalamus stimulation frequency controls cortical excitation/inhibition balance”).

References cited:

Cruikshank, S.J., H. Urabe, A.V. Nurmikko, and B.W. Connors, Pathway-specific feedforward circuits between thalamus and neocortex revealed by selective optical stimulation of axons. Neuron, 2010. 65(2): p. 230-45.

Galarreta, M. and S. Hestrin, Frequency-dependent synaptic depression and the balance of excitation and inhibition in the neocortex. Nat Neurosci, 1998. 1(7): p. 587-94.

claims.claim: 40 and 100 Hz stimulations of central thalamus caused widespread activation of forebrain, including frontal cortex, sensorimotor cortex, and striatum.
claims.source: 40 and 100 Hz stimulations of central thalamus caused widespread activation of forebrain, including frontal cortex, sensorimotor cortex, and striatum, and transitioned the brain to a state of arousal in asleep rats.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by the fMRI data presented in Figure 2B-C and quantified in Figure 2E-H, showing significantly greater activation volumes at these frequencies.

claims.claim: 40 and 100 Hz stimulations of central thalamus transitioned the brain to a state of arousal in asleep rats.
claims.source: 40 and 100 Hz stimulations of central thalamus caused widespread activation of forebrain, including frontal cortex, sensorimotor cortex, and striatum, and transitioned the brain to a state of arousal in asleep rats.
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral and EEG data in Figure 6, showing that high-frequency stimulations caused animals to awaken and exhibited low voltage fast EEG patterns.

claims.claim: 10 Hz stimulation evoked significantly less activation of forebrain compared to 40 and 100 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: In contrast, 10 Hz stimulation evoked significantly less activation of forebrain, inhibition of sensory cortex, and behavioral arrest.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the fMRI activation maps in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2E-H, showing significantly smaller activation volumes at 10 Hz.

claims.claim: 10 Hz stimulation evoked inhibition of sensory cortex.
claims.source: In contrast, 10 Hz stimulation evoked significantly less activation of forebrain, inhibition of sensory cortex, and behavioral arrest.
claims.evidence: This is supported by negative BOLD signals in Figure 2A and Figure 3A-B, and confirmed by electrophysiology showing decreased neuronal firing in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: 10 Hz stimulation evoked behavioral arrest.
claims.source: In contrast, 10 Hz stimulation evoked significantly less activation of forebrain, inhibition of sensory cortex, and behavioral arrest.
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations in Figure 6A showing absence seizure-like freezing in 4/7 animals during 10 Hz stimulation.

claims.claim: 10 Hz, but not 40 Hz, stimulation of central thalamus evoked spindle-like oscillations in zona incerta.
claims.source: To investigate possible mechanisms underlying the frequency-dependent cortical inhibition, we performed recordings in zona incerta, where 10, but not 40, Hz stimulation evoked spindle-like oscillations.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by field potential recordings in Figure 4D-E, showing significantly more spindle-like oscillations during 10 Hz stimulation.

claims.claim: Suppressing incertal activity during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation reduced the evoked cortical inhibition.
claims.source: Importantly, suppressing incertal activity during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation reduced the evoked cortical inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by combined optogenetic experiments in Figure 5G-H, showing that 50/76 cortical neurons exhibited reduced inhibition when eNpHR was activated in zona incerta during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation.

claims.claim: The central thalamus and intralaminar nuclei play a critical and unique function in regulating arousal, attention, and goal-directed behavior.
claims.source: The central thalamus and intralaminar nuclei, in particular, have been postulated to play a critical and unique function in regulating arousal, attention, and goal-directed behavior (Schiff and Pfaff, 2009; Mair et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Direct and indirect electrical stimulations of central thalamus control cortical EEG dynamics and elicit behavioral transitions between drowsiness/relaxation and wakefulness/attention.
claims.source: This idea dates back to the first demonstrations that direct and indirect electrical stimulations of central thalamus control cortical electroencephalography (EEG) dynamics and elicit behavioral transitions between drowsiness/relaxation and wakefulness/attention (Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949; Hunter and Jasper, 1949; Fuster, 1958).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical studies.

claims.claim: There is a monosynaptic pathway from the mesencephalic reticular formation to the central lateral (CL) and paracentral (PC) nuclei of central thalamus that projects to cerebral cortex and striatum.
claims.source: Steriade and Glenn (Steriade and Glenn, 1982) identified a monosynaptic pathway from the mesencephalic reticular formation to the central lateral (CL) and paracentral (PC) nuclei of central thalamus that projects to cerebral cortex and striatum.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The central thalamus receives projections from norepinephrinergic innervation from locus coeruleus.
claims.source: In addition to this input, the central thalamus receives projections from other arousal systems, including norepinephrinergic innervation from locus coeruleus (Vogt et al., 2008) and cholinergic innervation from the upper brainstem and basal forebrain (Heckers et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The central thalamus receives cholinergic innervation from the upper brainstem and basal forebrain.
claims.source: In addition to this input, the central thalamus receives projections from other arousal systems, including norepinephrinergic innervation from locus coeruleus (Vogt et al., 2008) and cholinergic innervation from the upper brainstem and basal forebrain (Heckers et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Virtually all relay cells of the CL nucleus project to both striatum and cerebral cortex.
claims.source: For example, virtually all relay cells of the CL nucleus project to both striatum and cerebral cortex (Deschenes et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Variations in the level of activity within the intralaminar nuclei are linked to changes in behavioral alertness.
claims.source: First, variations in the level of activity within the intralaminar nuclei are linked to changes in behavioral alertness (Kinomura et al., 1996; Shirvalkar et al., 2006; Mair and Hembrook, 2008; Schiff et al., 2013; Giber et al., 2015), including transitions during the normal sleep–wake cycle and acute cognitive enhancements such as improved working-memory and sustained attention (Baker et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to physiological studies.

claims.claim: Lesions of the central thalamus can produce enduring cognitive impairments, including reduced attentional processing and memory.
claims.source: Similarly, lesions of the central thalamus can produce enduring cognitive impairments, including reduced attentional processing and memory (Guberman and Stuss, 1983; Mair et al., 1998; Van Der Werf et al., 1999; Newman and Burk, 2005), hypersomnolence (Bassetti et al., 1996), or even coma (Castaigne et al., 1981; Plum, 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to lesion studies.

claims.claim: Lesions of the central thalamus can produce hypersomnolence.
claims.source: Similarly, lesions of the central thalamus can produce enduring cognitive impairments, including reduced attentional processing and memory (Guberman and Stuss, 1983; Mair et al., 1998; Van Der Werf et al., 1999; Newman and Burk, 2005), hypersomnolence (Bassetti et al., 1996), or even coma (Castaigne et al., 1981; Plum, 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical studies.

claims.claim: Lesions of the central thalamus can produce coma.
claims.source: Similarly, lesions of the central thalamus can produce enduring cognitive impairments, including reduced attentional processing and memory (Guberman and Stuss, 1983; Mair et al., 1998; Van Der Werf et al., 1999; Newman and Burk, 2005), hypersomnolence (Bassetti et al., 1996), or even coma (Castaigne et al., 1981; Plum, 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claims.claim: Neuronal loss across central thalamus has been associated with severely disabled and vegetative patients following severe traumatic brain injury.
claims.source: Indeed, neuronal loss across central thalamus has been associated with severely disabled and vegetative patients following severe traumatic brain injury (Maxwell et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical studies.

claims.claim: Electrical stimulation of the central thalamus at low frequencies is associated with absence seizures and behavioral arrest in animal models.
claims.source: In addition, electrical stimulation of the central thalamus at low frequencies is associated with absence seizures and behavioral arrest in animal models (Hunter and Jasper, 1949) and human subjects (Velasco, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous stimulation studies.

claims.claim: Electrical stimulation of the central thalamus at low frequencies is associated with absence seizures and behavioral arrest in human subjects.
claims.source: In addition, electrical stimulation of the central thalamus at low frequencies is associated with absence seizures and behavioral arrest in animal models (Hunter and Jasper, 1949) and human subjects (Velasco, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to human studies.

claims.claim: Anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness is associated with disrupted thalamocortical functional connectivity in regions consistent with the intralaminar nuclei.
claims.source: Human imaging studies have also found that anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness is associated with disrupted thalamocortical functional connectivity in regions consistent with the intralaminar nuclei (Akeju, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to human imaging studies.

claims.claim: 35% of cells identified within the bulk injection area were EYFP-positive.
claims.source: Of cells identified within the bulk injection area, 35% were EYFP-positive, and 97% of EYFP-positive cells co-expressed CaMKIIa, indicating high sensitivity for stimulation of excitatory neurons (n = 2 rats, 831 cells; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured from immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 97% of EYFP-positive cells co-expressed CaMKIIa.
claims.source: Of cells identified within the bulk injection area, 35% were EYFP-positive, and 97% of EYFP-positive cells co-expressed CaMKIIa, indicating high sensitivity for stimulation of excitatory neurons (n = 2 rats, 831 cells; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured from immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The CaMKIIa promoter is expressed primarily in excitatory neurons, the vast majority of which in thalamus are relay cells.
claims.source: This promoter is expressed primarily in excitatory neurons, the vast majority of which in thalamus are relay cells (Smith, 2008; Ellender et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on promoter expression.

claims.claim: Stimulation at all three frequencies (10, 40, and 100 Hz) resulted in a robust positive BOLD signal at the site of stimulation that was highly synchronized to light delivery.
claims.source: Indeed, stimulation at all three frequencies resulted in a robust positive blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal at the site of stimulation that was highly synchronized to light delivery, increased upon optical activation, and gradually returned to baseline following the end of stimulation (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the time series data in Figure 1E showing synchronized BOLD responses.

claims.claim: Stimulations at 10, 40, and 100 Hz all resulted in robust increases in the local neuronal firing rate at central thalamus.
claims.source: In agreement with the fMRI signal, stimulations at 10, 40, and 100 Hz all resulted in robust increases in the local neuronal firing rate (Figure 1G; n = 5 neurons, p< 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test between the 20 s pre-stimulation and stimulation periods, 12 trials for each neuron).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 1G with statistical significance.

claims.claim: The frequency of stimulation was a critical parameter in determining the extent of ipsilateral and contralateral BOLD activation.
claims.source: Both locally in the thalamus and at downstream, synaptically connected brain regions, the frequency of stimulation was a critical parameter in determining the extent of ipsilateral and contralateral BOLD activation – defined here as positive BOLD signals significantly synchronized to the block stimulation paradigm (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the differential activation patterns shown in Figure 2A-C and quantified in Figure 2E-H.

claims.claim: A much larger volume of brain tissue was activated by stimulation at 40 and 100 Hz compared to 10 Hz, with frontocortical areas and striatum being strongly activated at high frequencies.
claims.source: In general, a much larger volume of brain tissue was activated by stimulation at 40 and 100 Hz compared to 10 Hz, with frontocortical areas and striatum being strongly activated at high frequencies (Figure 2A–C; Videos 1–3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the activation maps in Figure 2A-C and quantified in Figure 2E-H.

claims.claim: The difference in activation volume between low- (10 Hz) and high- (40 or 100 Hz) stimulation frequencies was significant at the thalamus, striatum, and medial prefrontal, lateral prefrontal, cingulate, motor, and sensory cortices.
claims.source: This difference in activation volume between low- (10 Hz) and high- (40 or 100 Hz) stimulation frequencies was significant at the thalamus, striatum, and medial prefrontal, lateral prefrontal, cingulate, motor, and sensory cortices (Figure 2E–H).
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2E-H with statistical significance indicated.

claims.claim: Striatal activity was primarily localized to the dorsal sector, with negligible activity occurring in the ventral region.
claims.source: Striatal activity was primarily localized to the dorsal sector, with negligible activity occurring in the ventral region (Figure 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the activation maps in Figure 2B-C.

claims.claim: BOLD activation was generally restricted to the ipsilateral hemisphere.
claims.source: Furthermore, BOLD activation was generally restricted to the ipsilateral hemisphere, although activation volumes in the contralateral striatum, lateral prefrontal cortex, motor cortex, and sensory cortex were all significantly greater during 100 Hz stimulation compared to 10 Hz stimulation (Figure 2F–H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the activation maps in Figure 2 and quantified in Figure 2F-H.

claims.claim: Activation volumes in the contralateral striatum, lateral prefrontal cortex, motor cortex, and sensory cortex were all significantly greater during 100 Hz stimulation compared to 10 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: Furthermore, BOLD activation was generally restricted to the ipsilateral hemisphere, although activation volumes in the contralateral striatum, lateral prefrontal cortex, motor cortex, and sensory cortex were all significantly greater during 100 Hz stimulation compared to 10 Hz stimulation (Figure 2F–H).
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Figure 2F-H with statistical significance.

claims.claim: The somatosensory cortex exhibited a strong negative BOLD signal during 10 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: Despite targeted activation of excitatory neurons, the somatosensory cortex exhibited a strong negative BOLD signal during 10 Hz stimulation, suggesting a suppression of baseline activity (Figures 2A and 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the activation maps in Figure 2A and time series in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: Central thalamus stimulations at 40 and 100 Hz led to positive changes in the BOLD signal at the somatosensory cortex.
claims.source: In stark contrast, central thalamus stimulations at 40 and 100 Hz led to positive changes in the BOLD signal at the somatosensory cortex (Figures 2B,C and 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the activation maps in Figure 2B-C and time series in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: Stimulation of the same excitatory population at different frequencies resulted in completely opposite responses at a downstream target.
claims.source: Thus, stimulation of the same excitatory population at different frequencies resulted in completely opposite responses at a downstream target.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the negative BOLD at 10 Hz and positive BOLD at 40/100 Hz in somatosensory cortex shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: 10 Hz stimulation resulted in a decrease in neuronal firing rate in somatosensory cortex.
claims.source: In agreement with the BOLD activity observed during ofMRI experiments, 10 Hz stimulation resulted in a decrease in neuronal firing rate between pre-stimulation and stimulation periods (Figure 3D,E; n = 10 of 11 recorded neurons).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: Stimulations at 40 and 100 Hz both led to increases in neuronal firing in somatosensory cortex.
claims.source: Conversely, stimulations at 40 and 100 Hz both led to increases in neuronal firing (Figure 3D,E; n = 11 of 11 recorded neurons).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: The decrease in firing rate during 10 Hz stimulation occurred primarily over the interval from 5 to 15 s after stimulation began.
claims.source: Interestingly, the decrease in firing rate during 10 Hz stimulation occurred primarily over the interval from 5 to 15 s after stimulation began, while the increase in firing rate during 40 Hz stimulation occurred primarily over the first 10 s (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the temporal analysis presented in Table 1.

claims.claim: The increase in firing rate during 40 Hz stimulation occurred primarily over the first 10 s.
claims.source: Interestingly, the decrease in firing rate during 10 Hz stimulation occurred primarily over the interval from 5 to 15 s after stimulation began, while the increase in firing rate during 40 Hz stimulation occurred primarily over the first 10 s (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the temporal analysis presented in Table 1.

claims.claim: The increase in neuronal firing rate during 100 Hz stimulation was generally maintained throughout the 20 s stimulation period.
claims.source: On the other hand, the increase in neuronal firing rate during 100 Hz stimulation was generally maintained throughout the 20 s stimulation period (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the temporal analysis presented in Table 1.

claims.claim: Spike events occurring during inhibition had a non-uniform distribution over time, which peaked between 6 and 34 ms after light onset.
claims.source: Peri-stimulus time histograms also revealed that spike events occurring during inhibition had a non-uniform distribution over time, which peaked between 6 and 34 ms after light onset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the peri-stimulus time histograms in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The glutamatergic thalamocortical input at 10 Hz sometimes generated action potentials.
claims.source: These data suggest that the glutamatergic thalamocortical input at 10 Hz sometimes generated action potentials.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the peri-stimulus time histogram data showing spike events during 10 Hz stimulation.

claims.claim: Not every light pulse resulted in an immediate action potential during 10 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: Notably, however, not every light pulse resulted in an immediate action potential.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the spike fidelity data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing less than 100% fidelity.

claims.claim: Out of 28 isolated ZI neurons, the majority exhibited increases in their firing rate during central thalamus stimulation at both 10 and 40 Hz.
claims.source: Out of 28 isolated ZI neurons, the majority exhibited increases in their firing rate during central thalamus stimulation at both 10 and 40 Hz (Figure 4C; n = 26 and 22, respectively; p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test between the 20 s pre-stimulation and stimulation periods, 20 trials for each neuron).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 4C with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Large, amplitude-modulated spindle-like oscillations (SLOs) in the field potential occurred significantly more often during 10 Hz stimulation than 40 Hz stimulation in zona incerta.
claims.source: However, a key difference was that large, amplitude-modulated spindle-like oscillations (SLOs) in the field potential occurred significantly more often during 10 Hz stimulation than 40 Hz stimulation (Figure 4D,E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by field potential recordings in Figure 4D-E with statistical significance.

claims.claim: The spindle-like oscillations exhibited an inter-event interval centered around 6.6 ± 0.2 s.
claims.source: These oscillations exhibited an inter-event interval centered around 6.6 ± 0.2 s (s.e.m.), similar to those observed in thalamus during sleep onset (Contreras et al., 1997) (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Simultaneous EEG recordings in frontal cortex revealed strong spike-wave modulation during 10 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: Consistent with this, simultaneous EEG recordings in frontal cortex revealed strong spike-wave modulation during 10 Hz stimulation and lower amplitude, fast oscillations during 40 Hz stimulation, which are associated with loss of consciousness and aroused brain states, respectively (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the EEG recordings in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Simultaneous EEG recordings in frontal cortex revealed lower amplitude, fast oscillations during 40 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: Consistent with this, simultaneous EEG recordings in frontal cortex revealed strong spike-wave modulation during 10 Hz stimulation and lower amplitude, fast oscillations during 40 Hz stimulation, which are associated with loss of consciousness and aroused brain states, respectively (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the EEG recordings in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: EYFP-expressing axons were observed in ZI.
claims.source: EYFP-expressing axons were also observed in ZI (Figure 4H), indicating that central thalamus relay neurons may have direct connections to ZI and providing a possible anatomical substrate for these responses.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the fluorescence imaging in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Central thalamus relay neurons may have direct connections to ZI.
claims.source: EYFP-expressing axons were also observed in ZI (Figure 4H), indicating that central thalamus relay neurons may have direct connections to ZI and providing a possible anatomical substrate for these responses.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of EYFP-expressing axons in ZI shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Delivery of 593 nm light resulted in a decrease in firing for 62 out of 70 ZI neurons.
claims.source: Among the 70 neurons recorded in ZI, delivery of 593 nm light resulted in a decrease in firing for 62 cells (p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test between 20 s pre-stimulation period and 20 or 30 s stimulation period, 15–20 trials for each neuron), indicating that illumination of halorhodopsin was successful in suppressing incertal activity.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings with statistical significance.

claims.claim: When halorhodopsin activation in ZI was paired with 10 Hz stimulation of central thalamus, the previously described increase in incertal firing was disrupted.
claims.source: When halorhodopsin activation in ZI was paired with 10 Hz stimulation of central thalamus, the previously described increase in incertal firing (Figure 4C) was disrupted.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 5E-F.

claims.claim: In 60 out of 70 neurons, the difference in incertal firing rate between the 20 s 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation period and the pre-stimulation period was significantly reduced with concurrent eNpHR activation.
claims.source: In 60 out of 70 neurons, the difference in incertal firing rate between the 20 s 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation period and the pre-stimulation period was significantly reduced with concurrent eNpHR activation (Figure 5F; p < 0.05, one-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test, n = 10–20 trials).
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5F with statistical significance.

claims.claim: 68 out of 76 somatosensory cortex cells (89%) exhibited a decrease in firing during 10 Hz stimulation of central thalamus.
claims.source: Consistent with the data presented in Figure 3, 68 cells (89%) exhibited a decrease in firing during 10 Hz stimulation of central thalamus (uncorrected p < 0.05, Wilcoxon signed rank test; 10–15 trials for each neuron).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Suppression of ZI activity with eNpHR reversed the cortical inhibition effect during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation.
claims.source: Strikingly, however, suppression of ZI activity with eNpHR reversed this effect.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 5G-H.

claims.claim: 50 out of 76 neurons (66%) exhibited reduced inhibition when central thalamus stimulation was paired with eNpHR activation.
claims.source: Across animals, 50 out of 76 neurons (66%) exhibited reduced inhibition when central thalamus stimulation was paired with eNpHR activation (Figure 5H; p < 0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test over 1 s bins; 10–20 trials for each neuron).
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5H with statistical significance.

claims.claim: A fraction of cells switched from inhibitory responses to excitatory ones when ZI was suppressed during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation.
claims.source: Indeed, a fraction of cells switched from inhibitory responses to excitatory ones.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 5G-H showing reversal of inhibition.

claims.claim: mCherry-positive axons were observed in the sensory cortex.
claims.source: In support of this influence being through direct anatomical connections, mCherry-positive axons were observed in the sensory cortex (Figure 5I), consistent with previous reports of incerto-cortical projections (Lin et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the fluorescence imaging in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: Incertal activity during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation has a net inhibitory effect on somatosensory cortex.
claims.source: Collectively, these data suggest that incertal activity during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation has a net inhibitory effect on somatosensory cortex.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined optogenetic experiments showing that suppressing ZI reduces cortical inhibition.

claims.claim: During 10 Hz stimulation, the majority of animals exhibited behavior indicative of an absence seizure, including freezing and behavioral arrest throughout stimulation followed by a return to sleep.
claims.source: During 10 Hz stimulation, the majority of animals exhibited behavior indicative of an absence seizure, including freezing and behavioral arrest throughout stimulation followed by a return to sleep (Figure 6A; n = 4/7).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral observations in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The most common EEG response during 10 Hz stimulation was a transition to slow spike-wave discharges.
claims.source: In addition, the most common EEG response was a transition to slow spike-wave discharges (Figure 6B,C; n = 5/7), which are typically associated with loss of consciousness (Mirsky and VanBuren, 1965).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by EEG recordings in Figure 6B-C.

claims.claim: Stimulations at 40 and 100 Hz resulted in behavioral transitions to an awake state, reflected by exploration and goal-directed movement.
claims.source: In stark contrast, stimulations at 40 and 100 Hz resulted in behavioral transitions to an awake state, reflected by exploration and goal-directed movement (Figure 6A; n = 4/7 and 4/6, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral observations in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The most common EEG pattern evoked by 40 and 100 Hz stimulations was a low voltage fast response.
claims.source: Similarly, the most common EEG pattern evoked by these high-frequency stimulations was a low voltage fast response (Figure 6B; n = 3/7 and 6/6, respectively), indicative of cortical activation and desynchronization.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by EEG recordings in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The slow spike-wave and low voltage fast EEG responses evoked during behavioral experiments match those recorded under anesthetized conditions.
claims.source: Moreover, the slow spike-wave and low voltage fast EEG responses evoked during behavioral experiments (Figure 6C,D) match those recorded under anesthetized conditions (Figure 4G), further linking the network activation patterns revealed by ofMRI to the arousal responses reported here, as well as those reported in early stimulation studies (e.g. [Hunter and Jasper, 1949]).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing EEG patterns in Figure 6C-D with Figure 4G.

claims.claim: High-frequency EEG patterns evoked during 40 and 100 Hz stimulation associate with robust activation of frontal cortex, motor cortex, somatosensory cortex, and striatum.
claims.source: Notably, high-frequency EEG patterns evoked during 40 and 100 Hz stimulation associate with robust activation of frontal cortex, motor cortex, somatosensory cortex, and striatum – regions that receive widespread glutamatergic projections from intralaminar nuclei (Jones and Leavitt, 1974; Berendse and Groenewegen, 1990; Groenewegen and Berendse, 1994; Smith et al., 2004; Hoover and Vertes, 2007; Hunnicutt et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the fMRI data in Figure 2B-C and the EEG data in Figure 6, supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Slow-wave oscillations evoked during 10 Hz stimulation are associated with limited forebrain activation and strong inhibition of somatosensory cortex.
claims.source: On the other hand, slow-wave oscillations evoked during 10 Hz stimulation are associated with limited forebrain activation and strong inhibition of somatosensory cortex.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the fMRI data in Figure 2A and the EEG data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The frequency-dependent generation of spindle-like oscillations suggests that these differences may in part be due to the engagement of thalamocortical networks responsible for sleep and loss of perceptual awareness during 10 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: The frequency-dependent generation of spindle-like oscillations, which are known to underlie brain synchronization at the onset of sleep (Steriade et al., 1993), suggest that these differences may in part be due to the engagement of thalamocortical networks responsible for sleep and loss of perceptual awareness during 10 Hz stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the spindle-like oscillations observed in Figure 4D-F and supported by citation to sleep literature.

claims.claim: ZI sends direct GABAergic projections to somatosensory thalamic nuclei and sensory cortex.
claims.source: Anatomically, ZI sends direct GABAergic projections to somatosensory thalamic nuclei and sensory cortex (Nicolelis et al., 1995; Kolmac and Mitrofanis, 1999; Barthó et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claims.claim: ZI has been shown to selectively gate sensory information processing in higher order thalamic nuclei through GABAergic inhibition.
claims.source: Functionally, ZI has also been shown to selectively gate sensory information processing in higher order thalamic nuclei through GABAergic inhibition (Trageser and Keller, 2004; Lavallée et al., 2005; Trageser et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to functional studies.

claims.claim: Stimulation at 10 Hz in asleep rats evoked absence seizure-like freezing and spike-waves in a majority of animals.
claims.source: Stimulation at this frequency in asleep rats also evoked absence seizure-like freezing and spike-waves in a majority of animals, a cortical pattern known to be modulated by ZI projections (Shaw et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral and EEG data in Figure 6, supported by citation to ZI literature.

claims.claim: Rhythmic incertal activity contributes to membrane hyperpolarizations and sustained high-voltage cortical rhythms through GABAergic incertofugal pathways.
claims.source: Indeed, it has been previously suggested that rhythmic incertal activity contributes to membrane hyperpolarizations and sustained high-voltage cortical rhythms through GABAergic incertofugal pathways (Shaw et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Activity in ZI may act to limit forebrain activation through incertal-thalamic feedback.
claims.source: Given the presence of GABAergic projections from ZI to central thalamus (Barthó et al., 2002), activity in ZI may also act to limit forebrain activation, as observed with ofMRI during 10 Hz stimulation, through incertal-thalamic feedback.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the presence of GABAergic projections and the observed limited forebrain activation at 10 Hz.

claims.claim: Previous tracing studies failed to identify thalamic input specifically from intralaminar nuclei to ZI.
claims.source: However, we note that previous tracing studies failed to identify thalamic input specifically from intralaminar nuclei to ZI (Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous tracing studies.

claims.claim: Arousal regulation driven by central thalamus has a causal and frequency-dependent influence on ZI.
claims.source: In summary, our findings provide the first demonstration that arousal regulation driven by central thalamus has a causal and frequency-dependent influence on ZI, and that suppressing the recruitment of ZI modulates the brain-wide dynamics driven by central thalamus stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined optogenetic experiments in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The frequency-dependent depression of cortical activity is in part mediated by extrinsic inhibitory signals originating from ZI.
claims.source: Specifically, our results suggest that the frequency-dependent depression of cortical activity is in part mediated by extrinsic inhibitory signals originating from ZI.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined optogenetic experiments showing that suppressing ZI reduces cortical inhibition during 10 Hz stimulation.

claims.claim: Feedforward thalamocortical inhibition is the process by which relay neurons drive inhibitory post-synaptic potentials (IPSPs) in pyramidal cells via fast spiking cortical interneurons.
claims.source: An additional mechanism that could contribute to the evoked suppression of cortex is feedforward thalamocortical inhibition – the process by which relay neurons drive inhibitory post-synaptic potentials (IPSPs) in pyramidal cells via fast spiking cortical interneurons (Agmon and Connors, 1991; Porter et al., 2001; Cruikshank et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on thalamocortical inhibition.

claims.claim: Low-frequency (10 Hz) stimulations of certain thalamic nuclei in vivo yield strong hyperpolarization of cortical neurons putatively via feedforward thalamocortical inhibition.
claims.source: Low-frequency (10 Hz) stimulations of certain thalamic nuclei in vivo yield strong hyperpolarization of cortical neurons putatively via this process (Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1996a; 1996c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology studies.

results.result: High-frequency (40 and 100 Hz) optogenetic stimulation of central thalamus excitatory neurons causes widespread forebrain activation and behavioral arousal. fMRI shows significantly greater activation volumes in frontal cortex, motor cortex, sensory cortex, and striatum at 40/100 Hz compared to 10 Hz, with activation primarily ipsilateral but some contralateral recruitment at 100 Hz. Electrophysiology confirms increased local thalamic firing at all frequencies. Behavioral experiments show that 40/100 Hz stimulation transitions asleep rats to wakefulness with low-voltage fast EEG patterns indicative of arousal.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C26-C30, C32-C33, C63-C64, C66 provide converging evidence from fMRI (Figure 2B-H), electrophysiology (Figure 1G), and behavioral/EEG data (Figure 6) demonstrating that high-frequency stimulation drives widespread forebrain activation and arousal. The quantification shows statistically significant differences between frequencies with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05). Sample sizes are adequate (n=10-16 animals for fMRI, n=4-6 for behavior).

results.result: Low-frequency (10 Hz) stimulation of central thalamus causes limited forebrain activation, inhibition of somatosensory cortex, and behavioral arrest. fMRI shows significantly smaller activation volumes and negative BOLD signals in somatosensory cortex at 10 Hz. Electrophysiology confirms decreased neuronal firing in somatosensory cortex during 10 Hz stimulation (10/11 neurons), contrasting with increased firing at 40/100 Hz (11/11 neurons). Behavioral experiments show absence seizure-like freezing in 4/7 animals with spike-wave EEG patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C34-C38, C61-C62, C67 provide strong converging evidence from fMRI (Figures 2A, 3A-B), electrophysiology (Figure 3D-E, Table 1), and behavioral/EEG data (Figure 6) demonstrating frequency-dependent inhibition. The negative BOLD signal is validated by decreased neuronal firing with appropriate statistics (p<0.05, Wilcoxon tests). The opposite cortical responses at different frequencies from the same excitatory population represent a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: Low-frequency (10 Hz) but not high-frequency (40 Hz) central thalamus stimulation evokes spindle-like oscillations in zona incerta. Field potential recordings show significantly more spindle-like oscillations during 10 Hz stimulation (11/12 channels, p<0.01), with inter-event intervals of 6.6±0.2 s similar to sleep-onset oscillations. Simultaneous EEG shows spike-wave modulation at 10 Hz versus low-voltage fast oscillations at 40 Hz, suggesting engagement of sleep-related thalamocortical networks at low frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C45-C49, C68 are supported by field potential recordings (Figure 4D-F) and simultaneous EEG (Figure 4G) with appropriate statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.01). The spindle-like oscillations are well-characterized with quantified inter-event intervals. The link to sleep networks is supported by citation to prior literature and the observed EEG patterns. Sample size (n=2 animals, 28 neurons, 12 channels) is modest but adequate for this mechanistic finding.

results.result: Suppressing zona incerta activity with halorhodopsin during 10 Hz central thalamus stimulation reduces cortical inhibition, demonstrating a causal role for ZI in frequency-dependent cortical suppression. Optogenetic inhibition of ZI successfully suppressed firing in 62/70 neurons and disrupted the increase in ZI firing evoked by central thalamus stimulation (60/70 neurons, p<0.05). Critically, this ZI suppression reduced cortical inhibition in 50/76 somatosensory cortex neurons (66%, p<0.05), with some cells switching from inhibitory to excitatory responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C52-C57, C60, C75-C76 provide strong causal evidence through combined optogenetic manipulation (Figure 5). The dual-opsin approach (ChR2 in central thalamus, eNpHR in ZI) with simultaneous electrophysiology demonstrates that ZI mediates cortical inhibition. Statistics are appropriate (Wilcoxon tests, p<0.05) with adequate sample sizes (n=4 animals, 70 ZI neurons, 76 cortex neurons). This represents a novel mechanistic finding linking central thalamus arousal circuits to ZI.

results.result: Anatomical evidence supports direct connections between central thalamus and zona incerta, and between ZI and sensory cortex. EYFP-expressing axons from central thalamus were observed in ZI (Figure 4H), and mCherry-positive axons from ZI were observed in sensory cortex (Figure 5I). Prior literature establishes that ZI sends GABAergic projections to somatosensory thalamus and cortex and gates sensory information processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51, C59, C69-C70, C73 are supported by fluorescence imaging (Figures 4H, 5I) and citations to anatomical literature. The observed axonal projections provide anatomical substrate for the functional effects. However, the claim of direct connections from central thalamus to ZI (C51) is somewhat tentative as prior tracing studies failed to identify such connections (C74), though the fluorescence data suggests they exist. The anatomical evidence supports but does not fully prove monosynaptic connectivity.

results.result: Optogenetic targeting achieved specific stimulation of excitatory relay neurons in central thalamus with appropriate spatial restriction. Immunohistochemistry shows 35% of cells in the injection area were EYFP-positive, and 97% of EYFP-positive cells co-expressed CaMKIIa (n=2 rats, 831 cells). Optical parameters indicate stimulation volume of 0.08 mm³. Fluorescence imaging confirms projections to frontal cortex and striatum, primarily ipsilateral, with superficial layer convergence in cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25, C102-C106 provide methodological validation of the optogenetic approach. The immunohistochemistry data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) confirms specificity for excitatory neurons. The optical calculations are based on cited assumptions (Aravanis et al., 2007) and are reasonable. The anatomical projections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) match known central thalamus connectivity. This validation is essential for interpreting the functional results.

results.result: The temporal dynamics of cortical responses differ across stimulation frequencies. During 10 Hz stimulation, decreased firing occurred primarily 5-15 s after onset, while 40 Hz-induced increases occurred in the first 10 s, and 100 Hz increases were maintained throughout the 20 s period. Peri-stimulus time histograms show that during 10 Hz stimulation, spike events peaked 6-34 ms after light onset, suggesting some thalamocortical inputs generated action potentials despite net inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by temporal analysis in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The temporal differences suggest frequency-dependent short-term plasticity. The peri-stimulus analysis reveals that not every 10 Hz pulse evokes spikes, indicating complex integration. Statistics are appropriate (Wilcoxon tests, uncorrected p<0.05). This provides mechanistic insight into how frequency modulates cortical responses.

results.result: Direct stimulation of central thalamus excitatory neurons at different frequencies leads to opposite BOLD signals (positive at 40/100 Hz, negative at 10 Hz) that are coupled with corresponding changes in neuronal activity (increased vs. decreased firing). This validates that negative BOLD signals reflect decreases in neuronal activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by combined fMRI and electrophysiology (Figure 3) showing tight coupling between BOLD signals and neuronal firing. This addresses an important question about the neural basis of negative BOLD signals. The finding is consistent with prior literature (cited Shmuel et al., 2006; Huttunen et al., 2008) and extends it by using optogenetic stimulation of a defined population.

results.result: Control experiments with constant 3 ms pulse width across frequencies (10, 40, 100 Hz) preserved the frequency-dependent increase in cortical and striatal activation, demonstrating that stimulation frequency rather than pulse width is the primary factor modulating forebrain fMRI activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by control experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B) with n=3 animals. The preserved frequency effects when pulse width is held constant rule out pulse width as a confound. This control is important because the main experiments used different pulse widths (30, 7.5, 3 ms) to maintain constant 30% duty cycle. The control validates the interpretation that frequency is the key parameter.

results.result: The frequency-dependent forebrain activation pattern is specific to central thalamus. Stimulation of other thalamic nuclei (ventral posteromedial, anterior, posterior) failed to evoke similarly widespread striatal and cortical activity. Stimulation of intermediate hippocampus also did not show large differences in forebrain activation between 10 and 40 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are supported by control experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B) comparing central thalamus to other targets. This demonstrates regional specificity and strengthens the conclusion that the observed effects are not simply due to any subcortical stimulation. However, sample sizes for control targets are not specified, which is a limitation.

results.result: EEG patterns evoked during behavioral experiments (spike-wave at 10 Hz, low-voltage fast at 40/100 Hz) match those recorded under anesthetized conditions, linking the fMRI activation patterns to arousal responses. Pre-stimulus EEG band power was consistent across frequencies, confirming similar baseline states.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C117 are supported by comparing EEG patterns in Figures 6C-D with Figure 4G, and by band power analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). This validates that the anesthetized fMRI experiments are relevant to awake behavior. The consistent baseline EEG across frequencies is important for ruling out pre-existing state differences.

results.result: Feedforward thalamocortical inhibition via cortical interneurons may contribute to cortical suppression during 10 Hz stimulation, in addition to the demonstrated role of ZI. Prior literature shows that low-frequency stimulation of thalamic nuclei causes cortical hyperpolarization, and that matrix thalamocortical neurons preferentially drive layer I interneurons with sustained IPSPs during repeated stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 are based on citations to prior literature (Agmon and Connors, 1991; Castro-Alamancos and Connors, 1996a/c; Cruikshank et al., 2012) and speculation (C82). While the authors acknowledge this as a possible mechanism, they provide no direct experimental evidence for interneuron-mediated inhibition in their study. The peri-stimulus data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is consistent with this mechanism but does not prove it. This remains a hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: The current study's results are partially consistent with prior work by Logothetis et al. showing frequency-dependent BOLD responses in thalamic stimulation, but differ in that no significant negative BOLD signals were observed in polysynaptically connected cortical regions during high-frequency stimulation. Corticocortical disynaptic inhibition is unlikely to drive the observed 10 Hz cortical suppression given its bias toward higher frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 appropriately contextualize the findings relative to prior work (Logothetis et al., 2010; Silberberg and Markram, 2007). The comparison is supported by the data (Figure 2B-C showing predominantly positive BOLD at high frequencies). The reasoning about corticocortical inhibition being unlikely at 10 Hz is logical given the cited frequency bias. This discussion appropriately identifies similarities and differences with prior work.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation allowed selective excitation of a single group of excitatory neurons and identification of their frequency-dependent role in network function, overcoming limitations of electrical stimulation which cannot dissociate effects of stimulation frequency from preferential recruitment of different neuronal populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 are supported by the experimental design and results throughout the manuscript. The optogenetic approach (CaMKIIa promoter for excitatory neurons) provides cell-type specificity that electrical stimulation lacks (cited McIntyre and Grill, 2002). The frequency-dependent effects observed (Figures 2-6) demonstrate the value of this approach. This is a valid methodological advantage.

results.result: The ofMRI approach reveals dramatic frequency-dependent differences in global brain dynamics and supports central thalamus as a target for remediating cognitive disabilities via forebrain recruitment. The ofMRI techniques are generalizable to study DBS mechanisms for other targets and disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by the dramatic differences in activation patterns shown in Figure 2 and the widespread forebrain recruitment at high frequencies. The translational relevance to DBS is reasonable given the clinical context discussed. The generalizability of ofMRI methods (C98) is a valid statement about the technique's applicability, though it is somewhat speculative regarding future applications.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that central thalamus and intralaminar nuclei play critical roles in arousal, attention, and goal-directed behavior, with anatomical connections from brainstem arousal systems and widespread projections to cortex and striatum. Physiological studies link intralaminar activity to behavioral alertness, while lesions cause cognitive impairments, hypersomnolence, or coma. Low-frequency electrical stimulation is associated with absence seizures in animals and humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C22 are all supported by citations to prior literature and provide appropriate background context. These claims accurately represent the cited work and establish the scientific foundation for the current study. They are not novel findings but rather a synthesis of established knowledge that motivates the experimental questions.

results.result: Previous tracing studies failed to identify thalamic input specifically from intralaminar nuclei to zona incerta, creating some uncertainty about the anatomical pathway despite the observed EYFP-expressing axons in ZI.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 is supported by citation to Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1985. This creates a tension with the observed EYFP axons in ZI (C50), which the authors acknowledge. The discrepancy could reflect limitations of prior tracing methods, viral spread to adjacent nuclei, or polysynaptic connections. The authors appropriately note this uncertainty.

results.result: Methodological details include use of female Sprague-Dawley rats, challenges in targeting small intralaminar nuclei leading to exclusion of animals with inaccurate implants (2/18 excluded for lack of fMRI activity), identification of ZI based on depth, spike latencies, and whisker receptive fields, and 24% eNpHR transfection efficiency in ZI.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101, C115-C116 are methodological details stated in the Materials and methods section. The exclusion criteria (C101) are clearly stated and appropriate. The ZI identification criteria (C115) are reasonable and supported by citation (Nicolelis et al., 1992). The transfection efficiency (C116) is directly measured. These details are important for reproducibility.

results.result: fMRI acquisition used 23 coronal slices with 0.5×0.5 mm² in-plane resolution, 0.5 mm thickness, and 750 ms frame rate using spiral k-space trajectories and sliding window reconstruction for high spatiotemporal resolution with whole-brain coverage.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 is a methodological detail about fMRI parameters stated in Materials and methods and supported by citation (Fang and Lee, 2013). These parameters are appropriate for whole-brain rodent fMRI and represent good spatiotemporal resolution. This is important for understanding the quality and coverage of the imaging data.
